## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Saṅgārava Sutta* (MN 100) depicts an encounter between the Buddha and the young brahmin student Saṅgārava, who approaches the Buddha after becoming irritated by a brahmin woman's open devotion to him [SuttaCentral]. Saṅgārava questions the Buddha regarding the epistemological grounds on which he teaches the holy life [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. In response, the Buddha distinguishes himself from traditionalists (*anussavika*)—who ground their doctrine in oral transmission and Vedic tradition—as well as from pure reasoners, asserting that his teaching stems from his own direct experience and higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) of truths never heard before (*pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu*) [Anālayo, Genesis of the bodhisattva ideal; Anālayo 2018; Freedman 1977; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; SuttaCentral]. During the conversation, the Buddha is also questioned about the existence of the *deva*s [Polak 2011].
To demonstrate this direct realization, the Buddha delivers an autobiographical exposition of his pre-awakening quest [Anālayo 2018]. He recalls his initial reflection on the constricted nature of household life compared to the freedom of renunciation (*sambādho gharāvāso rajāpatho, abbhokāso pabbajjā*) [Anālayo, Genesis of the bodhisattva ideal; Bareau, La jeunesse du Buddha; Polak 2011], followed by his training under Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta [Gaffney 2003; Wynne, The origin of Buddhist meditation]. He then recounts his arrival at Uruvelā and his severe ascetic practices—including breathless meditation, crushing mind with mind, and extreme emaciation—all of which he ultimately rejected as ineffective [Bronkhorst 1993; Wynne, The origin of Buddhist meditation]. Turning instead to the four meditative absorptions (*jhāna*s), he attained the three higher knowledges (*tevijjā* / *abhiññā*): the recollection of past births, the divine eye perceiving the rebirth of beings, and the destruction of the taints (*āsava*s) [Anālayo 2018; Gaffney 2003]. Unlike the *Bodhirājakumāra Sutta* (MN 85), which continues into post-awakening events, the autobiographical narrative in MN 100 concludes at the attainment of awakening [Polak 2011].
Specific parallel phrasing and episodes are attested in Sanskrit fragments (such as SHT sutta40 and fragment 348r) [Anālayo, Genesis of the bodhisattva ideal; Anālayo 2018; SuttaCentral], as well as in broader narrative literature aligned by DharmaNexus and SuttaCentral, including the *Mahāvastu*, the *Lalitavistara*, the *Saṅghabhedavastu*, the Tibetan *Abhiniṣkramaṇasūtra*, and parallels in the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 101) and *Ekottarāgama* (EĀ 31.8) [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral].
